title: Beginner’s Guide to Highschool iGEM: Research Fundamentals
byline: Prepared By: Humza Shahzad, ULP-CA 2026 Co-Founder and Student Lead
raw_pages:
Beginner’s Guide to Highschool iGEM: 
Research Fundamentals 
 
Prepared By: Humza Shahzad, ULP-CA 2026 Co-Founder and 
Student Lead 
 
Foreword 
 
Hello Everyone, my name is Humza Shahzad and I am the Co-Founder of the new 
ULP-CA iGEM team competing in iGEM 2026. I’m a high school student in 
Fullerton, CA with a burning curiosity for the possibilities that synthetic biology 
can bring us one day. I hope this guide finds people that too want to start their 
research journey with more knowledge than I first had, once requiring hundreds of 
hours of reading research papers and designing experiments with my team to 
understand the fundamentals of biotech research. I’ve condensed the basics into 
this document and hope that all that read it truly appreciate it, as this is a testament 
to the very beginnings of my biotech journey and hopefully the start of yours. 
Onwards padawans! 
 
The Basics:  
 
DNA : Deoxyribose nucleic acid, a type of macromolecule (fancy talk for a BIG 
molecule, in which case DNA is pretty long). Uses ATCG to store the code for 
PROTEINS, one of the most important macromolecules in synbio! 
 
Proteins: A very large macromolecule; made up of subunits called amino acids. 
Each amino acid corresponds to a codon, a group of 3 base pairs that is read when 
RNA is built using DNA as a template for protein production(outside of the 
nucleus!)  
 
Protein Functions: Proteins are unique in that they serve the majority of active 
functions in the body. Proteins move muscle cells to contract, catalyze chemical 
reactions(these are enzymes!! ), embed in the cell membrane to act as 
receptors(immune cells anybody??), act as functional compounds (e.g. silk, hair, 
mucus, etc.), or serve regulatory functions (hemoglobin/myoglobin as oxygen 
transporters).  
 
SynBio Starter Guide! 
 
 
What makes Synbio so special? Synthetic biology essentially focuses on utilizing 
biology for certain functions. This is important in fields such as the pharmaceutical 
industry such as the development of a new drug, and using rigorous testing 
procedures in order to begin and pass clinical trials.  
 
DBTL, or Design, Build, Test, and Learn is the reason why bioengineering gets to 
be called an engineering discipline. Simply, like engineers, scientists of synthetic 
biology have an engineering goal and create an initial design of their system, 
construct it(typically through recombinant gene assembly methods), run 
tests/assays on it, and use the information from this cycle to LEARN, therefore 
starting the next cycle. A good synthetic biologist always documents their 
engineering decisions like a normal engineer would. Ample data collection is 
meant to be informative for a scientist to rule out problems within their design 
through thought-out experiments that maintain good positive and negative controls. 
This is what makes science DEFENSIBLE.  
 
Before we start, here is something very important that many people get wrong 
when they first start working with synbio. Biology is a heuristic system, not a 
binary one. By this I mean the following: heuristics is a concept in computer 
science that effectively means “good enough”. Biology is the product of millions 
upon millions of years of careful evolution, and we have acquired information 
about biology after very rigorous study. However, changing the delicate system of 
biology on the molecular level comes with its own implications, in the sense that 
nothing is a yes or a no. A mutation in a protein can make it semi-functional but 
not fully non-functional. A weak promoter could mean that less but not near none 
of a gene is transcribed. Introducing elements that are foreign into a bacterial 
genome could have implications that we won’t know how to rule out unless we 
have good experiments, because biology doesn’t necessarily follow all of the rules! 
Biological systems make mistakes, and that is the beauty of it. If they didn’t, then 
we wouldn’t have diseases and genetic defects now would we?  
 
 
Gene Design Principles 
 
 
In order to understand how to design a synthetic biology project, we must 
understand a few things about coding regions and sequences in DNA that don’t 
code for proteins.  
 
There are key parts to a gene besides the coding region, the sequence with all 
necessary codons for a protein. These parts come in the following order:  
 
1.​ Promoter: Determines how strongly a gene is expressed in terms of the 
amount of protein expressed and how rapidly. The standard unit for a 
promoter’s strength is Relative Promoter Units(RPU). Promoter sequences 
are the first sequence recognized by RNA Polymerase to start DNA 
transcription into an mRNA sequence.  
 
2.​ Ribosome Binding Site(RBS): A non-coding region included in the final 
mRNA sequence. It is where a ribosome will first bind to mRNA before 
RNA translation.  
 
3.​ Start Codon: The first codon of RNA that initiates protein production during 
RNA translation. The start codon ALWAYS corresponds to the methionine 
amino acid.  
 
4.​ Coding Region: Self-explanatory :) 
 
5.​ Stop Codon: Signals the ribosome to detach from the mRNA molecule.  
 
6.​ Terminator: Usually placed twice in the gene in synthetic biology 
experiments, as it ensures that RNA polymerase detaches from DNA during 
transcription completely.  
 
Key Tip: Thanks to the UC Berkeley iGEM team, we have a characterized library 
of promoters called Anderson Promoters, all which have varying strengths at 
relatively common levels used in experiments, such as 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, etc. I highly 
recommend considering the use of Anderson Promoters in your experiments 
because they are perfect for tuning of a system in terms of gene expression.  
 
 
Now, although this system for protein production works, there is a fatal flaw. If one 
were to follow the framework for a gene above, experiments would probably not 
go so well in terms of protein function. This is because the promoter is in a 
constitutive form, meaning that it is ALWAYS on. Usually, we are engineering 
bacteria, and we must not forget that bacteria have other stuff to care about besides 
our insignificant little gene. Making a gene constitutive means that it will not stop 
the protein production process, and that uses copious amounts of ATP and other 
cellular resources that cause metabolic stress, which can contribute to protein 
misfolding and ultimately the very death of our cells. So what do we use? We use 
the operon architecture, made up of an operator and a repressor.  
 
 
Fig. 1 Operon Architecture. Source(bio.libretexts.org)  
 
With reference to Fig.1, an operon architecture is different from a normal gene 
architecture in that we observe the use of an operator and regulatory sequence(also 
known as the repressor). The regulatory sequence is a separately expressed gene 
that creates a repressor protein that binds to the operator sequence. By binding to 
the operator sequence, it acts as a roadblock for RNA polymerase, and the genes 
following the operator aren’t able to be transcribed. This is the “OFF” state for our 
genes. In order to switch our gene into the “ON” state, bacteria must first be grown 
to a certain density in a phase called log phase with an optical density at 600 nm, or 
OD600, between 0.4 and 0.6. Don’t worry about this for now, but it is very 
important once you step into the lab and your PI uses this term when teaching you 
bacterial culture. Now, where were we?  
 
 
After the bacteria have reached an optimal growth phase, we add a solution of an 
inducing molecule. Besides containing a site to bind to the operator, repressor 
proteins also have a site that binds to an inducer molecule, causing a change in the 
shape of the repressor that forces it to detach from the DNA. In some cases, the 
“inducer” molecule is actually a “corepressor” molecule, in the sense that when it 
binds to the repressor protein, it actually ENABLES it to bind to the operator. 
When the concentration of a corepressor molecule decreases, so does the amount 
of its operator-bound repressor proteins, therefore causing us to observe the “ON” 
state of our gene.  
 
TLDR:  
Inducer System: Inducer + Repressor = ON 
Corepressor System: Corepressor + Repressor = OFF 
Besides basic protein expression, it's important to use operator and repressor 
systems because it gives us something valuable: CONTROL. If we create a genetic 
circuit, a network of genes expressed separately, operons allow us to control how 
the expression of one gene affects another. For example, one gene can create an 
enzyme that produces two byproducts, one of which contributes to a therapeutic 
and another which acts as the inducer molecule for another operon, and so on. An 
operon can also be used as an on/off switch to gene expression.  
 
Gene Assembly + Testing 
 
Alright so gene structure is great and all but what's the point? How do we actually 
take a gene we have designed and test it in a cell? For the most part, high school 
iGEM teams tend to dabble only in bacteria and bacterial DNA. But why is that? 
 
Bacteria have their own genome as well as large, circular pieces of DNA called 
plasmids that they can take up from their environment, or in a solution if you 
utilize heat shock or electroporation methods. This is how bacteria pass genes from 
one to another in a process called horizontal gene transfer. Scientists have taken 
advantage of this inherent feature of bacteria and created bacterial plasmids that are 
optimized as templates for gene expression.  
 
There are two types of plasmids and they differ based on the way they replicate:  
 
 
❖​1. Expression Plasmid:  
➢​These are plasmids that are optimized for protein expression. They 
contain a sequence called an origin of replication(ori) like any 
plasmid that gives them a low copy number. That is, fewer copies of 
the plasmid are made because copying a plasmid is a metabolically 
stressful process, especially when our main goal is to produce a 
protein.  
➢​The pET series, namely pET-28(a), is the most common expression 
plasmid used. It has a T7 promoter, which is an incredibly strong 
promoter attached to the lac operon induced by the chemical IPTG.  
➢​The recommended cell line for protein expression is BL21(DE3), 
especially when using a T7 promoter because only BL21(DE3) cells 
possess the correct T7 polymerase to recognize its corresponding 
promoter.  
❖​Cloning Plasmid 
➢​These are plasmids optimized for cloning. Their ori is of a high copy 
number since the goal is to make more copies of the DNA. There is no 
template for gene architecture in a cloning plasmid, so don’t be 
alarmed since our goal is not to express a gene.  
➢​Why do we need to make more though? Sometimes, when we order 
DNA sequences to be synthesized, we don’t have enough for our 
desired experiments. So, we insert our coding sequences into a 
cloning plasmid to produce more copies of our cloning sequence. 
Then, we use restriction enzymes to cut out our coding sequences and 
insert them into an expression plasmid.  
 
Restriction Enzymes: When DNA sequences become Legos.  
 
When several DNA coding sequences are cloned in different plasmids and they 
need to be put into a singular plasmid, we must use restriction enzymes to cut out 
DNA at precise locations such that each cut strand is assembled into one plasmid 
by the hydrogen bonds made between base pairs. EcoRI is a common Type II 
restriction enzyme that cuts at an EcoRI site in DNA, highlighted in yellow in Fig. 
2.  
 
 
 
​
Fig. 2 Diagram of EcoRI Type II Restriction Enzyme 
 
If you observe the way that EcoRI cuts at its recognition site, you can see that it 
leaves an overhang of 4 DNA base pairs. These are called sticky ends such that 
they will “stick” to another complementary 4 base pair overhang in another 
plasmid. Using Type II restriction enzymes is useful for gene insertion when two 
enzymes are used, since using the same restriction enzyme for the forward and 
reverse strand would prevent us from knowing the orientation the DNA has aligned 
in, and the wrong protein would be expressed if the DNA was reversed. This is 
called a double digest. This may be tricky to visualize, so I recommend watching 
this video from the wonderful people at Waterloo iGEM here. You may also 
reference Fig. 3.  
 
 
 
Fig. 3 Single VS. Double Digests. Source: SnapGene 
 
Well what if we have multiple fragments of DNA we need to assemble? What if we 
have multiple promoters, ribosome binding sites, coding sequences, and 
terminators that all need to be put into a specified order? That’s where my favorite 
kind of assembly method comes in: Golden Gate Assembly. Golden Gate 
Assembly is a DNA assembly method that uses a special Type IIS restriction 
enzyme to assemble multiple fragments of DNA into a plasmid using only one 
enzyme.  
 
The reason this works is due to the mechanism of a Type IIS restriction enzyme. 
Like any restriction enzyme, Type IIS restriction enzymes have recognition sites. 
However, instead of cutting DNA at the restriction site, Type IIS enzymes cut 
OUTSIDE of the recognition site, producing a very unique 4 base pair overhang. If 
you design your DNA fragments to have matching overhangs, you can 
 
theoretically assemble hundreds of DNA fragments at once without leaving a 
restriction “scar”, a nonfunctional sequence of DNA left behind from a restriction 
digest.  
 
 
Fig. 4 Golden Gate Assembly. Source: NEB 
 
The Lab and Onwards!  
 
 
Everything I’ve explained and attempted to teach is all usable in theory. However, 
in order to properly execute experiments and protocols in a laboratory, it is up to 
you to decide what procedures you need to follow. Thankfully, processes like DNA 
purification, protein purification, DNA assembly, and running assays are all 
well-laid out on sites such as New England Biolabs, SnapGene, and even the old 
iGEM parts registry .Here are some useful links that will help you draft up your 
own protocols with your mentors:  
 
New England Biolabs Protocol Search: 
https://www.neb.com/en-us/tools-and-resources/search?type=Protocol 
 
Journey of Visualized Experiments:  
https://www.jove.com/ 
 
OpenWetWare:  
https://openwetware.org/wiki/Main_Page 
 
Best of luck with your research my fellow iGEMers. Now fly! ;) 
 
 
 
-​
Humza Shahzad, ULP-CA 2026 Co-Founder

blocks.text: ❖Cloning Plasmid
blocks.html: ❖Cloning Plasmid

blocks.text: ➢These are plasmids optimized for cloning. Their ori is of a high copy number since the goal is to make more copies of the DNA. There is no template for gene architecture in a cloning plasmid, so don’t be alarmed since our goal is not to express a gene.
blocks.html: ➢These are plasmids optimized for cloning. Their ori is of a high copy number since the goal is to make more copies of the DNA. There is no template for gene architecture in a cloning plasmid, so don’t be alarmed since our goal is not to express a gene.

blocks.text: ➢Why do we need to make more though? Sometimes, when we order DNA sequences to be synthesized, we don’t have enough for our desired experiments. So, we insert our coding sequences into a cloning plasmid to produce more copies of our cloning sequence. Then, we use restriction enzymes to cut out our coding sequences and insert them into an expression plasmid.

blocks.text: Restriction Enzymes: When DNA sequences become Legos.

When several DNA coding sequences are cloned in different plasmids and they need to be put into a singular plasmid, we must use restriction enzymes to cut out DNA at precise locations such that each cut strand is assembled into one plasmid by the hydrogen bonds made between base pairs. EcoRI is a common Type II restriction enzyme that cuts at an EcoRI site in DNA, highlighted in yellow in Fig. 2.

EcoRI is a common Type II restriction enzyme that cuts at an EcoRI site in DNA, highlighted in yellow in Fig. 2.

blocks.alt: EcoRI recognition and cleavage sites with complementary sticky ends.

blocks.text: Fig. 2 Diagram of EcoRI Type II Restriction Enzyme
blocks.html: Fig. 2 Diagram of EcoRI Type II Restriction Enzyme

blocks.text: If you observe the way that EcoRI cuts at its recognition site, you can see that it leaves an overhang of 4 DNA base pairs. These are called sticky ends such that they will “stick” to another complementary 4 base pair overhang in another plasmid. Using Type II restriction enzymes is useful for gene insertion when two enzymes are used, since using the same restriction enzyme for the forward and reverse strand would prevent us from knowing the orientation the DNA has aligned in, and the wrong protein would be expressed if the DNA was reversed. This is called a double digest. This may be tricky to visualize, so I recommend watching this video from the wonderful people at Waterloo iGEM here. You may also reference Fig. 3.

blocks.text: Well what if we have multiple fragments of DNA we need to assemble? What if we have multiple promoters, ribosome binding sites, coding sequences, and terminators that all need to be put into a specified order? That’s where my favorite kind of assembly method comes in: Golden Gate Assembly. Golden Gate Assembly is a DNA assembly method that uses a special Type IIS restriction enzyme to assemble multiple fragments of DNA into a plasmid using only one enzyme.
blocks.html: Well what if we have multiple fragments of DNA we need to assemble? What if we have multiple promoters, ribosome binding sites, coding sequences, and terminators that all need to be put into a specified order? That’s where my favorite kind of assembly method comes in: Golden Gate Assembly. Golden Gate Assembly is a DNA assembly method that uses a special Type IIS restriction enzyme to assemble multiple fragments of DNA into a plasmid using only one enzyme.

blocks.text: The reason this works is due to the mechanism of a Type IIS restriction enzyme. Like any restriction enzyme, Type IIS restriction enzymes have recognition sites. However, instead of cutting DNA at the restriction site, Type IIS enzymes cut OUTSIDE of the recognition site, producing a very unique 4 base pair overhang. If you design your DNA fragments to have matching overhangs, you can theoretically assemble hundreds of DNA fragments at once without leaving a restriction “scar”, a nonfunctional sequence of DNA left behind from a restriction digest.

blocks.text: The Lab and Onwards!

Everything I’ve explained and attempted to teach is all usable in theory. However, in order to properly execute experiments and protocols in a laboratory, it is up to you to decide what procedures you need to follow. Thankfully, processes like DNA purification, protein purification, DNA assembly, and running assays are all well-laid out on sites such as New England Biolabs, SnapGene, and even the old iGEM parts registry .Here are some useful links that will help you draft up your own protocols with your mentors:
